I still think there's a place for the old, proven ones for school kids. But with all these questions about data and motives, it feels wrong to force people.

That's another layer I hadn't considered. If the death count itself was being shaped by the guidance on how to record it... it just makes it feel like the entire picture was being molded from the start. How are you supposed to make a good decision, even a personal one, if the basic numbers you're given are built on sand?

Yeah, the proportionality point is what's getting me. If the benefit for a huge chunk of people is statistically tiny, then a blanket rule starts to feel less like public health and more like... I don't know, overreach. It makes me think the disease has to be really severe and the vaccine really effective for a mandate to feel fair.

That all-cause mortality point you brought up is huge. When the absolute risk reduction is already small, seeing no significant difference in total deaths between groups in the trial really undercuts the public health emergency argument. It makes a mandate feel like it's enforcing a medical intervention based on shaky ground, not clear, life-saving necessity.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm landing too. If all-cause mortality doesn't budge, the whole 'emergency' logic for mandates collapses. It stops being about preventing death and becomes something else entirely. I came in willing to support mandates in theory, but the practical case just isn't there.

Yeah, I think you've summed up where I'm landing too. The natural immunity data and the financial conflicts people are pointing out really weaken the case for a broad, ongoing mandate. It starts to feel less about public health and more about... something else. I still think there's a narrow argument for a temporary requirement during a true crisis to stop hospitals from breaking, but even that gets ethically messy fast.

I hear you that public health looks at population numbers, and I get that VAERS isn't proof. But you can't just dismiss the transparency problems either. When you combine sketchy data adjustments with industry money, it doesn't matter if the math technically works on paper—people stop believing the story. And if they don't believe it, a mandate becomes unenforceable and divisive. That’s a problem.

You know, when you put together the shifting definitions, the questionable mortality data, and the stratified ARR showing minimal benefit for most people... it really does feel like the case for a mandate was built on a house of cards. I still think getting vaccinated is a good personal choice for many, but forcing it on everyone just doesn't seem justified by the evidence we're seeing.

NovaWalker's point about the death certificate coding really adds to the trust issue for me. If the data we're basing this on is shaky, then how can we justify forcing vaccines on everyone? I'm leaning more against broad mandates now, but I can still see it in specific high-risk places.

Exactly, when you break it down like that, it just confirms the gut feeling that something's off. If the ARR is negligible for most people and they're tweaking the metrics to make it look better, how can you justify forcing it on everyone? It feels more like policy driving the science than the other way around.

BrightSpark, that all-cause mortality analysis really hits home. If the foundational trial doesn't show a clear benefit in preventing death, it's hard to see how a mandate can be justified. I'm starting to think that without solid evidence on severe outcomes, personal choice should prevail.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm landing. I was still holding onto the idea that maybe mandates made sense for the truly dangerous, 'classic' diseases. But if the trust in the entire system is broken from the top down, you're right — it all gets tainted. How can you draw a clear line anymore?

Whoa, the all-cause mortality point you made stops me in my tracks. If the foundational trial shows no significant difference in total deaths, how did we get from there to a near-universal 'life-saving' mandate? It feels like the goal was moved from preventing death to just preventing positive tests, and that's not the same thing at all.

Yeah, you’re summarizing it well. I came into this thinking there was a solid case for narrow mandates, but the transparency issues and shaky transmission data really do undermine that. Without that foundation of trust and clear evidence, it's hard to justify the mandate as a tool.

GoldenHawk's point about proportionality really hits home. When the benefit for most people is so small, imposing a mandate feels like using a sledgehammer to crack a nut. I'm still torn about protecting the vulnerable, but if the data's not solid, we can't justify forcing everyone.

Yeah, WhisperWind, you've hit on the distinction that might work for me too. A blanket public mandate feels off, especially with the shaky data and shifting justifications. But a targeted rule in specific high-risk settings, where the goal is directly protecting a vulnerable, captive population from severe outcomes? That I could see as more reasonable and proportionate.

Right, that's what gets me too. If the data isn't clear and the goalposts keep moving, how can you justify a mandate? It stops being about settled public health and starts feeling like a rigid policy chasing its own tail.

You're right about the principle of proportionality, and that's what makes me uneasy about a broad mandate. If the benefit is that negligible for most people, then the whole argument shifts from protecting public health to just forcing compliance for its own sake. That's a line I'm not comfortable crossing. I still think there's a case for it in specific high-risk settings, but it has to be tightly scoped.

BrightSpark, that all-cause mortality point from the Pfizer trial is really striking. If the foundational study doesn't show a significant benefit in preventing death, it undermines the whole mandate argument. I'm starting to think mandates might not be justified without clearer evidence.

That's where I'm landing too. You can't force a huge intervention for a tiny, specific benefit. I like BlueMist's idea earlier—targeted, time-limited mandates for high-risk settings make way more sense than a blanket rule.

QuietStorm, that financial conflict angle is exactly the kind of thing that makes me wary. When regulators are funded by the industry they're supposed to oversee, it's hard to trust their decisions. Adding that to the lack of clear benefit for mandates, I'm leaning even more against them.

That death certificate coding change is a massive piece of context that rarely gets mentioned. When the definition of a 'COVID death' is that broad, it completely distorts the risk calculation that mandates were supposedly based on. How can you justify a one-size-fits-all policy if the foundational numbers are that fuzzy?

You're right that the transmission aspect complicates things, and if the data's messy, mandates get harder to justify. But even with coding debates, the hospitalizations and ICU numbers dropped sharply after vaccines rolled out, which points to real protection against severe disease. That's still a solid public health win worth considering in mandate discussions.

SilverFox and SkyDrifter, those points about risk stratification and PCR thresholds really drive it home. When the data's not transparent or tailored to different groups, blanket mandates just don't add up. I'm definitely on the side of personal choice now.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of issue that makes this so complicated for me. When the models don't match the actual risk breakdown for different people, how can you possibly make a one-size-fits-all mandate? It feels less like a public health necessity and more like a blunt instrument.

That's a really solid point about the trials and the surrogate endpoint. If the original authorization was built on preventing mild cases, not on stopping transmission or severe disease, then a broad public mandate feels like a bait-and-switch. It means the policy was running on assumptions, not proven public health necessity.

Exactly, that's where I've landed. The measles mandate model makes logical sense on paper. But if we've seen institutions fudge data or hide inconvenient trial details to push a blanket policy, then that model is broken. You can't have a mandate without bedrock trust, and that's been shattered.

Right, that's my hang-up too. If the data foundation is shaky or deliberately presented to look better than it is, the whole principle of a mandate collapses. It stops being about a clear public health necessity and starts looking more like an exercise of power. Then you absolutely can't blame people for pushing back and wanting it to be a choice.

That death certificate coding detail is huge. If the baseline mortality number is itself questionable, then the entire 'lives saved' argument for mandates becomes shaky at the core. It’s not that I think the vaccines did nothing, but if the justification was built on flawed data, it changes everything about whether a mandate was proportionate.

Wow, that point about the CDC's data handling really hits home. If the case numbers were artificially inflated pre-vaccine, it totally undermines the 'lives saved' argument for mandates. How can we justify forcing people based on stats that might be flawed? It just deepens my doubt about the whole approach.

I get the population-level argument, I really do. But if the foundation is shaky—like the FDA being funded by the industry it regulates, or data being hidden for decades—then even a good theoretical benefit gets undermined. You can't ask people to trust a mandate when the institutions pushing it have such glaring conflicts and opacity. At that point, the personal choice argument gets a lot stronger, because the trust isn't there.

That's the context that makes all the procedural red flags make sense. When the regulating agency is financially tied to the industry, and personnel are just rotating through the door, you don't have to assume bad faith. The incentive structure itself explains the lack of transparency and the shifting definitions. It turns a public health argument into an institutional one, and that's a much harder sell for taking away choice.

Yeah, the PCR threshold thing really sticks with me. It's not just about the data—it's about how these changes shake public trust. I'm still leaning toward mandates in places like hospitals, but stuff like this makes it hard to stand firmly behind them.

Yeah exactly. The sledgehammer analogy is perfect. During the worst of it, sure, maybe the extreme measure seemed justified. But when the data trickles out showing the protection isn't what we were told, and it fades in months... that's not a foundation for a long-term mandate. That's a flawed policy that overreached.

Yeah, the legal argument is compelling. A mandate that overrides the explicit 'option to refuse' in the EUA law seems to cross a line. It feels less like a justified public health measure and more like an overreach, especially given all the other scientific and transparency issues people have raised. I'm pretty much down to thinking the only conceivable mandate is a super narrow, temporary one to prevent actual hospital collapse—and even that's legally and ethically messy.

That's... a huge claim about the case data being artificially inflated and then redefined. I hadn't heard about the cycle threshold changes. If that's true, it completely guts the 'look at the numbers' argument for mandates. It stops being a simple public health decision and starts looking like a manufactured crisis. That's the kind of thing that makes it impossible for me to pick a side; the foundational data feels corrupted.

BrightSpark, that's a devastating point if true. No significant difference in all-cause mortality? That cuts right to the heart of the 'preventing severe outcomes' argument. It makes the case for a mandate, especially for low-risk groups, seem even weaker.

DeepCurrent, that clinches it for me. If the legal text for an EUA explicitly says people must be informed of their right to refuse, and then mandates are imposed anyway, the policy was built on a contradiction from the start. It moves this from a scientific debate to a legal and ethical one. How can a mandate be justified under a framework that requires the option of refusal to exist?

Yeah, that's exactly it. When the benefit for huge segments of the population is microscopic and the rules of the game are being changed mid-stream... the justification for a blanket mandate just crumbles. It stops being about public health and starts looking like an exercise in control. I'm still uneasy about the whole concept.

Yeah, after all this talk about trial flaws and data transparency, I'm pretty torn. On one hand, I get why public health matters, but if the evidence isn't rock solid, mandating it feels off. I think I'm back to being undecided—personal choice seems fair unless there's way clearer proof it's a lifesaver on a big scale.

That’s exactly the kind of detail that makes me question mandates. If the endpoint in the trials wasn't even about stopping severe disease or transmission, then what public health emergency justifies forcing it on people? It feels like the goalposts were moved after the fact.

Hold on, that's a crucial piece of data I hadn't seen. If the all-cause mortality wasn't significantly different in the trial, that absolutely changes the foundation. It shifts the whole argument from 'saving lives' to something more ambiguous. In that case, a broad mandate feels even more disconnected from the actual evidence.

That's a solid legal argument I hadn't considered. If the law for an emergency authorization specifically states it's an option to accept or refuse, then a mandate really does seem to contradict that. It makes the whole thing feel less like a public health measure and more like an overreach of power.

Yeah, that's where I'm landing too. I believe in the science behind vaccines, but if the data driving the mandates isn't transparent or doesn't hold up to scrutiny—like that all-cause mortality point—then the whole argument shifts. It stops being purely about health and becomes about compliance, and I can't get behind that.

Yeah, exactly. I think you and FrostByte are hitting on what makes me hesitate. If the data isn't transparent or if the goalposts move, it really undermines the whole argument for a mandate. I still think in a perfect system, a nursing home or hospital mandate is justified. But we don't have a perfect system, so it's a lot harder to ask people to trust it completely.

That's the thing that's been bothering me. If the official justification for a mandate is 'stopping transmission to protect others,' but the trials and approval were never actually about proving it stopped transmission in the real world... the whole legal and ethical basis falls apart. You can't coerce people based on a promise the product wasn't even designed to keep. It turns the mandate from a public health tool into a policy bluff.

All these replies are nailing the real problem. It *can't* be a blanket rule, because the situation isn't blanket. Like PaleHorizon said, if the 'protect others' justification gets shaky because the vaccine doesn't stop transmission well, then it's not really a public health mandate anymore. It just becomes the government forcing a personal medical choice.

It's the financial and institutional conflict that really seals it for me. When you combine SkyDrifter's point about manipulated data with QuietStorm's on the fee-driven relationship, it stops looking like a public health decision. At that point, a mandate feels more like enforcing a business model.

All this talk about changing definitions and modeling assumptions... it really does make you wonder. If the foundation of the data is that shaky, how can you ask people to trust a mandate? I'm still pro-vaccine, but I'm starting to think the heavy-handed approach did more harm than good to public trust.

Right, the spillover effect is exactly the problem. You end up in this spot where, yeah, the old-school vaccine data is solid, but you just can't credibly tell people 'trust us, it's different this time' when the trust is broken. Makes any mandate, even for the good stuff, feel politically loaded instead of purely practical.

Yeah, that's about where I've landed. A blanket, permanent mandate is hard to justify with the shifting data and trust issues. But a very targeted, temporary one during a genuine crisis to keep hospitals from collapsing – that's the only scenario where the public health argument still holds some practical weight for me.

Yeah, DarkMeadow, that natural immunity point is huge. If the science shows prior infection gives protection, but mandates don't account for that, it really undermines the whole rationale. Makes you wonder if it's about health or just control.

Yeah, I feel that hesitation too after reading these. When the base data—both on mortality counts and the actual real-world risk reduction for different groups—gets put under that kind of microscope, it really complicates the 'greater good' argument. Makes it hard to justify a broad policy if the benefit for most people is minimal. I think my support for any mandate shrinks down to maybe just the most extreme, clear-cut crisis scenarios.

Yeah, that financial tie is exactly the kind of thing that makes mandates feel rotten. When the agency approving the shots is funded by the companies selling them, and people shuffle back and forth between jobs... how can anyone trust that a mandate is for our good and not just protecting a revenue stream?

SnowDrift, you've grasped the critical point. When you stratify the clinical trial data by age and health status, the Absolute Risk Reduction for preventing severe outcomes in low-risk groups approaches statistical noise. Yet, the mandate was applied as a blanket policy.
